title: How to Think About the Midterms
summary:
On Tuesday, people across the United States will vote in midterm elections. These elections decide who controls Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate, in the middle of a president's term.

A recent poll asked people about money. 44 percent said their finances have mostly stayed the same. 38 percent said things have gotten worse. Only 15 percent said things have gotten better.

History can help us guess what may happen. Since World War Two, the president's party has gained seats in the House only twice in a midterm election. On average, it loses 26 seats. When a president's approval rating is below 50 percent, the average loss is 35 seats.

Recent polls point to gains for Democrats. They are favored to win control of the House and are within reach of the Senate. Still, analysts say the size of any gain is not clear.

One reason is the map. There are about 30 fewer competitive districts than in 2018, and redrawing district lines helped Republicans by about eight seats.

Turnout could decide close races. Most races will be called on election night, but some may take days or weeks.
why_it_matters: Elections decide who makes the rules that affect your school, your town and your family.
